title: Async streams and await using
sub: await foreach, generators, cancellation and DisposeAsync
cards/0/body:
IAsyncEnumerable<T> is an asynchronous sequence: items arrive one at a time, and you can wait between them. A method with async and yield return is called an async generator. The compiler accepts such a method only if it's declared as IAsyncEnumerable<T> (or IAsyncEnumerator<T>). With Task<List<T>> it's a compile error.

You read the sequence with await foreach. It waits for each next item the same way await waits for a task: while there's no item, the thread is free.

Unlike Task<List<T>>, you can process the first items right away, and you don't have to hold the whole list in memory.
cards/1/q: Why is IAsyncEnumerable<T> better than Task<List<T>>?
cards/1/options/0: You can process the first items without waiting for all of them to load
cards/1/explain: You don't have to keep a million lines from a file in memory at once: each one is processed while the next is being read.
cards/2/explain: await foreach waits for each next item without blocking the thread.
cards/3/body:
A generator is a state machine too (section 3), only it pauses not just at await but also at yield return. The compiler expands await foreach roughly as in the code below. Step by step:

  • 1. Calling ReadOrdersAsync() only creates an object. The generator's body hasn't run yet, and not a single line of the file has been read.
  • 2. The first MoveNextAsync starts the body and runs it to the first yield return. There may be awaits on the way: then MoveNextAsync returns an unfinished ValueTask<bool>, and the consumer waits with no thread.
  • 3. At yield return, MoveNextAsync completes with true, and the item is in Current. The generator stays parked at that yield.
  • 4. The next MoveNextAsync resumes the body after the yield, up to the next yield.
  • 5. The body is done: MoveNextAsync returns false, and the loop exits.
  • 6. DisposeAsync runs the generator's finally (that's where the file is closed), even if you left the loop with break or an exception.

Until the consumer asks for the next item, the generator stays put. That's built-in backpressure: a slow consumer won't let the generator run ahead and fill up memory.
cards/4/q: var orders = ReadOrdersAsync(); and nothing else. How many lines of the file have been read?
cards/4/options/0: None: the generator's body starts running on the first MoveNextAsync
cards/4/options/1: The whole file: an async method runs synchronously up to the first await
cards/4/options/2: One: the generator runs up to the first yield return
cards/4/explain: Calling a generator only creates the sequence object. The body is started by the first MoveNextAsync, and await foreach is what calls it. That's the difference from an ordinary async method, which runs its first MoveNext right away.
cards/4/wrong/1: That's how an async Task method behaves: builder.Start runs the first MoveNext immediately. A generator waits until someone asks it for an item.
cards/4/wrong/2: The body reaches the first yield only on the first MoveNextAsync, and nobody has called it yet.
cards/5/q: The consumer leaves await foreach with break after three orders. What happens to the finally inside the generator, where the file is closed?
cards/5/options/0: It runs right away: await foreach calls DisposeAsync, and that runs the generator's finally
cards/5/options/1: It runs when the GC collects the enumerator
cards/5/options/2: The generator first reads the rest of the file, then runs the finally
cards/5/explain: await foreach expands into a try/finally with await e.DisposeAsync(). Leaving the loop by any route calls DisposeAsync, and that runs the generator's finally from the yield where it was parked. The rest of the file isn't read.
cards/6/body:
You can pass a token to a generator as an ordinary parameter: ReadOrdersAsync(ct). But often one piece of code creates the sequence and another iterates it. Then the consumer passes the token with .WithCancellation(ct).

  • WithCancellation doesn't call the method again and doesn't touch its parameters. The token goes to GetAsyncEnumerator(ct).
  • The enumerator the compiler generated puts that token into the parameter marked with the [EnumeratorCancellation] attribute. If a token was passed both to the parameter and through WithCancellation, they're combined: canceling either one stops the generator.
  • Without the attribute, the token from WithCancellation has nowhere to go, and cancellation silently doesn't work. The compiler only warns: CS8425.

Inside the generator you pass the token further down, as in any async method (section 2).
cards/7/q: The generator's CancellationToken parameter has no attribute. The consumer writes .WithCancellation(cts.Token) and cancels. What happens?
cards/7/options/0: The generator never sees the cancellation: the token went to GetAsyncEnumerator, and without [EnumeratorCancellation] it wasn't put into ct
cards/7/options/1: The generator stops: WithCancellation passes the token to the first CancellationToken parameter
cards/7/options/2: A compile error: without the attribute you can't call WithCancellation
cards/7/explain: ct stays default, a token that will never be canceled. The compiler warns about this (CS8425) but doesn't forbid it. Mark the parameter with the [EnumeratorCancellation] attribute.
cards/7/wrong/1: WithCancellation doesn't touch the method's parameters: the token goes to GetAsyncEnumerator, and from there only into a parameter with the attribute.
cards/7/wrong/2: It's warning CS8425, not an error: the code compiles and silently doesn't cancel.
cards/8/body:
If cleaning up a resource is itself asynchronous (flushing a buffer to the network, closing a connection), the type implements IAsyncDisposable with a ValueTask DisposeAsync() method. await using calls it at the end of the block and waits for it with await: the thread isn't blocked while the cleanup runs.

The compiler expands it into a try/finally with an await inside the finally, as in the comment below. You've already seen this mechanism: at the end, await foreach calls DisposeAsync on the enumerator.

A plain using would call the synchronous Dispose. For network resources it can block the thread while the remaining data is sent.
cards/9/q: How is await using different from using?
cards/9/options/0: It calls DisposeAsync and waits for it with await, without blocking the thread
cards/9/options/2: It frees the object's memory right away, without waiting for the GC
cards/9/explain: A plain using would call the synchronous Dispose, which can block the thread. In both cases the GC frees the object's memory: Dispose and DisposeAsync release resources, not memory.
cards/10/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/10/options/1: An async method with yield return declared as IAsyncEnumerable<T> is an async generator
cards/10/options/2: The generator doesn't read the next item until the consumer asks for it
cards/10/options/4: await foreach loads all the items at once
cards/10/options/5: An async method with yield return can return Task<List<T>>
cards/10/explain: Items arrive one at a time, when the consumer asks. yield return in an async method is allowed only with IAsyncEnumerable<T> or IAsyncEnumerator<T>.
cards/11/pairs/1/1: Run the generator to the next yield
cards/11/pairs/3/1: The parameter that token lands in
